questions.q: What is the general size relationship between `node:20`, `node:20-slim`, and `node:20-alpine`?
options: They are all exactly the same size; the suffix only affects behavior, not size
node:20 is the largest (full Debian userland), node:20-slim is smaller, and node:20-alpine (Alpine Linux-based) is typically the smallest of the three
node:20-alpine is always the largest because it includes extra security tools
Size depends entirely on the application code, not the base image
questions.explain: The full node:20 image includes a complete Debian userland with many tools most apps never use. -slim strips much of that out, and -alpine, based on a smaller Linux distribution, is typically smaller still.

options: It prevents Docker from ever building the image
It excludes listed files and directories from the build context, so COPY can't pull them in and they're never sent to the Docker daemon
It automatically deletes files from the running container after startup
It only affects which files docker logs displays
questions.explain: Without a .dockerignore, everything in the build context (like a local node_modules or .git folder) is sent to the Docker daemon even if unused -- .dockerignore excludes it entirely, shrinking images and speeding up builds.

questions.q: Why doesn't deleting the apt cache in a separate, later `RUN` instruction reduce the final image size, compared to deleting it within the same `RUN` that created it?
options: Because apt caches cannot be deleted by any Docker instruction

Because each RUN produces its own layer, and a layer permanently retains everything written during it -- so the cache is already baked into the earlier layer and remains even after a later RUN removes the files
Because deleting files always increases image size due to metadata overhead
Because RUN instructions execute in a random, non-sequential order
questions.explain: Since each RUN creates its own immutable layer, files written and later deleted in a different RUN still occupy space in the earlier layer. Chaining install and cleanup into a single RUN avoids ever persisting that cache.

questions.q: What does `docker history northbridge/catalog:1.4` show you?
options: A log of every time the container has been started or stopped
The image's layers, listed with the instruction that created each one and its individual size, useful for finding which instruction is responsible for bloat
The git commit history of the application's source code
A list of every container ever created from this image
questions.explain: docker history breaks a built image down layer by layer, showing the creating instruction and size for each -- the tool to use when an image is bigger than expected.

questions.q: Why might a team hesitate before switching a production image straight to an `-alpine` base, despite the size savings?
options: Alpine images cannot run any application code at all
Alpine uses musl instead of glibc, which can occasionally cause compatibility issues with native modules that expect glibc
Alpine-based images are always larger in practice once running
Docker does not support running alpine-based images in production
questions.explain: Alpine Linux's musl-based libc differs from the glibc most native Node modules are built and tested against, which can occasionally cause compatibility issues worth checking before switching.
